title: Oscar and the Locker
premise: In the dying mill town of Halloway Bend, Xanthe Villalobos has survived high school by being exactly one thing: the only out kid in nine hundred people, and therefore untouchable, unpartnered, and unbothered. Then history teacher Ms. Okonkwo pairs him with Oscar Reyes—golden boy, wrestling captain, and the boy who once shoved him into a locker—to restore the town's founding time capsule before developers demolish the old schoolhouse. As they decode a century-old inheritance left by the town's queer founder, Xanthe realizes Oscar's hostility was always fear, and their uneasy alliance becomes something neither can name. When the demolition permit moves up and the town council votes to bury the founder's true story forever, Xanthe must choose between protecting his own hard-won invisibility and exposing everything—including himself—to save both the tradition and the boy he loves.
about_author: Casper Amberdale is the pen name of a former small-town debate coach who grew up in a town of fewer than a thousand people and never stopped writing about them. They live somewhere rural with two cats and an unreasonable collection of local-history pamphlets.

chapters.title: Nine Hundred Witnesses
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A wry tour of Halloway Bend: everyone knows everyone, and everyone knows Xanthe is gay, which he treats as armor rather than wound. He narrates his survival rules for small-town life. Emotional beat: defiant self-containment that readers will soon see is exhaustion wearing a costume.

chapters.title: The Assignment
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Ms. Okonkwo announces the semester capstone: document and preserve the Founder's Day time capsule before the schoolhouse demolition. She pairs students alphabetically-adjacent by seat. Xanthe turns and finds Oscar Reyes already scowling at him. Beat: dread sharpened by the humiliation of history repeating itself.

chapters.title: Locker Number 114
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, first time inside his head. The locker shove happened freshman year; Oscar has spent three years not thinking about it. Now he's forced to sit across from Xanthe twice a week. He tells himself it's nothing. Beat: guilt he refuses to name, established through what he avoids looking at.

chapters.title: Ground Rules
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The boys negotiate a hostile truce in the library: no personal questions, split the work, never be seen together outside class. Xanthe sets terms like a lawyer because control is safety. Beat: brittle comedy masking how much the proximity costs him.

chapters.title: What Elias Left Behind
chapters.summary: Dual-focus chapter, mostly Xanthe's POV. Research reveals town founder Elias Halloway sealed the capsule in 1923 with a sealed second letter 'for whoever the town could not yet hold.' The historical commission's records on Elias are suspiciously thin. Beat: first spark of real curiosity replacing resentment.

chapters.title: The River Road Detour
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Car trouble strands the pair together after a records trip; walking the river road, Oscar almost apologizes and instead asks why Xanthe 'makes everything about being gay.' Xanthe walks off. Beat: Oscar's defensiveness cracking against Xanthe's fury—and his own confusion about why he cares.

chapters.title: Grandmother Villalobos Knows Things
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At home, Xanthe's abuela mentions her own mother spoke of Elias Halloway's 'companion who was never called anything.' The family kept quiet for generations. Xanthe realizes the erasure is generational, deliberate. Beat: grief and kinship across a century; the theme of inheritance made intimate.

chapters.title: Practice, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Wrestling practice goes badly; Oscar snaps at teammates, then finds Xanthe waiting with research notes he didn't have to deliver personally. A teammate slurs Xanthe within earshot and Oscar—reflexively, shockingly—shuts it down. Beat: Oscar's loyalty splitting from his reputation.

chapters.title: The Sealed Letter
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. In the county archive they find the 1923 letter referenced but withheld: the historical society president, Dale Pruitt, controls access and wants the demolition approved quietly. First hint the 'tradition' is curated. Beat: injustice stops being abstract; the antagonist takes shape.

chapters.title: Detention Economics
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Both boys get detention after a hallway confrontation with Pruitt's grandson; stuck in one room, they play twenty questions to pass the hours. Oscar admits the locker thing wasn't random—someone dared him, and he wanted the excuse. Beat: the apology Xanthe never expected, landing without absolution yet.

chapters.title: Homecoming Is Mandatory
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Homecoming week spotlights both boys: Oscar crowned onto court, Xanthe enduring the annual 'good sport' performance of tolerance. Oscar watches Xanthe get mocked gently, publicly, and feels sick at his own past applause. Beat: love against duty begins its first open argument inside Oscar.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Post-game night at the riverbank, working late on the exhibit layout. A moment—shoulder to shoulder, breath visible in October cold—almost becomes something. Oscar pulls back, says 'this isn't—' and can't finish. Beat: yearning and terror in equal measure; the reader's heart breaks a little early.

chapters.title: Cold Shoulder Season
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Oscar ices him out at school; Xanthe pretends relief and fails. Abuela sees through him instantly. Meanwhile Pruitt fast-tracks the demolition vote using the project's own delay as evidence the capsule doesn't matter. Beat: loneliness compounded—the cost of wanting someone who won't stay.

chapters.title: Elias's Companion Has a Name
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Through church baptismal records and a photograph, Xanthe identifies Elias's companion: Thomas Iriarte, stonemason, listed on no monument. The capsule likely holds Thomas's letter—the town's erased queer founding heart. Beat: righteous purpose crystallizing; justice outside the law becomes the mission.

chapters.title: Oscar Breaks
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. His father finds Oscar's search history and the archive photos; a brutal dinner-table scene about 'what people will say.' Oscar realizes he's been raised to guard a legacy built on hiding. He bikes to Xanthe's house at midnight and says sorry properly this time. Beat: collapse and conversion; duty redefined.

chapters.title: The Plan Nobody Voted On
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The boys go rogue: copy archival evidence, contact a state historian, and plan to open the capsule legally via a preservation loophole Ms. Okonkwo hints at—but Pruitt moves the council vote up ten days. Beat: momentum and mounting stakes; the clock becomes a character.

chapters.title: Leak
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Someone tips Pruitt about the plan; Ms. Okonkwo is threatened with dismissal for 'politicizing curriculum,' and the town gossip machine brands Xanthe a troublemaker with an agenda. Even allies flinch. Beat: isolation at maximum pressure; Xanthe questions whether visibility was ever worth it.

chapters.title: What the Town Could Not Yet Hold
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Night before the vote, the boys break into the schoolhouse—not to steal, but to stand where Elias stood, and find Thomas's letter hidden separately in the cornerstone, addressed 'to the boy who is not allowed to exist yet.' They read it aloud together. Beat: hushed, sacred climax-of-feeling; a century of silence answered.

chapters.title: The Vote
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Council chamber packed. Pruitt frames the capsule as sentimental clutter; Oscar stands beside Xanthe in front of the whole town, reads Thomas Iriarte's letter aloud, and says plainly that he's done pretending about either the history or himself. Beat: public climax—love against duty resolved in speech, at cost.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Unscripted
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The vote splits; demolition delayed pending review, Ms. Okonkwo reinstated, Pruitt exposed falsifying records. But Oscar faces his father's cold house and teammates' silence. Xanthe waits for him anyway, on the porch, no conditions. Beat: victory that isn't free; tenderness after courage.

chapters.title: Founder's Day, Revised
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Spring: the capsule opens publicly, Thomas Iriarte added to the monument, the schoolhouse landmarked. Xanthe and Oscar walk in holding hands—not the only story in town anymore, just theirs. Beat: inheritance reclaimed; joy earned rather than granted.

chapters.title: Letter for Whoever Comes Next
chapters.summary: Shared final pages, alternating voice. The boys seal a new letter into the restored capsule—for the next kid in a town of nine hundred who needs proof they were always part of the founding. Final line echoes Thomas's letter. Beat: resolution as continuation; the tradition saved by changing what it means.
